{{short description|American film and television director, screenwriter, producer, actor (b. 1949)}} {{Use American English|date=March 2023}} {{Use mdy dates|date=March 2023}} {{Infobox person | name = Carl Franklin | image = Carl Franklin publicity photo from Fantastic Journey cast, 1977 (cropped).JPG | caption = Franklin in a publicity photo for ''[[The Fantastic Journey]]'' (1977) | birth_name = Carl Michael Franklin | birth_date = {{birth date and age|1949|4|11}} | birth_place = [[Richmond, California]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | occupation = Film director, television director, actor, screenwriter, television producer | education = [[University of California, Berkeley]] ([[Bachelor of Arts|BA]])
[[American Film Institute]] ([[Master of Fine Arts|MFA]]) | years_active = 1973–present }} '''Carl Michael Franklin''' (born April 11, 1949)[https://archive.today/20130125142206/http://www.hollywood.com/celebrity/189750/Carl_Franklin Carl Franklin {{pipe}} Biography, Photos, Movies, TV, Credits {{pipe}} Hollywood.com] is an American film and television director, producer, screenwriter, and former actor. He began his career in the 1970s as a television actor, playing regular roles as Dr. Fred Walters on ''[[The Fantastic Journey]],'' Detective Jerry Cross on ''[[McClain's Law]]'', and Captain Crane on ''[[The A-Team]]''. In the 1980s, he graduated from the [[AFI Conservatory]], and began directing B-movies at [[Roger Corman]]'s [[New Concorde|Concorde Pictures]]. His 1992 film ''[[One False Move]]'' (1992), written by and starring [[Billy Bob Thornton]], earned him the [[Independent Spirit Award for Best Director|Best Director Award]] at the [[8th Independent Spirit Awards]]. His subsequent cinematic directorial efforts include ''[[Devil in a Blue Dress (film)|Devil in a Blue Dress]]'' and ''[[Out of Time (2003 film)|Out of Time]];'' both starring [[Denzel Washington]], ''[[One True Thing]]'', ''[[High Crimes]],'' and ''[[Bless Me, Ultima (film)|Bless Me, Ultima]].'' Since the 2010s, most of his work has been for television, including shows such as: ''[[Rome (TV series)|Rome]]'', ''[[The Pacific (miniseries)|The Pacific]]'', ''[[The Newsroom (American TV series)|The Newsroom]]'', ''[[House of Cards (American TV series)|House of Cards]]'', ''[[Homeland (TV series)|Homeland]]'', ''[[The Affair (TV series)|The Affair]]'', ''[[The Leftovers (TV series)|The Leftovers]]'', ''[[13 Reasons Why]]'', ''[[Ray Donovan]]'', ''[[Mindhunter (TV series)|Mindhunter]],'' and the [[Ryan Murphy (producer)|Ryan Murphy]] production ''[[Monster (American TV series)|Monster]]''. His television accolades include a [[BAFTA TV Award]], two [[NAACP Image Awards]], and two [[Primetime Emmy Award]] nominations. ==Early life== Franklin was born and raised in [[Richmond, California]].{{Cite web |last=Goldstein |first=Patrick |date=September 24, 1995 |title=Easing Into Old L.A. |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1995-09-24-ca-49274-story.html |access-date=November 27, 2022 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}} He never had the opportunity to know his biological father, who had died before Carl was born. Franklin was raised by his mother and stepfather. While Franklin speaks highly of his stepfather and has called him "very loving",[http://www.answers.com/topic/carl-franklin Carl Franklin: Biography from Answers.com] he has spoken about his stepfather's abusive tendencies, linking his outbursts to alcohol use. Problems at home combined with life in a tough neighborhood fueled Franklin's ambition to be the first in his family to attend college. He was awarded a scholarship to [[University of California, Berkeley]]. Franklin's initial desires to become a teacher or lawyer led him to study history upon his arrival at the university. However, after two years, Franklin changed his major to theater arts. Franklin did not actively participate in the many demonstrations at Berkeley in the period. Describing the scene, Franklin told the ''[[Los Angeles Times]]'': "It was like a dream to me, I wasn't really sophisticated enough to join a particular movement." == Career == === Acting === After graduation, Franklin made his theater debut as a slave in [[The Public Theater]]'s production of ''[[Timon of Athens]]''. He would go on to act in [[Mark Taper Forum]]'s production of ''In the Belly of the Beast.'' One of his first jobs was acting in the [[New York Shakespeare Festival]], where he appeared in the ''Twelfth Night'' and ''Cymbeline''. Franklin began his on-screen career in the film ''[[Five on the Black Hand Side]]'' in 1973. From there, he acted in a string of guest roles on television shows such as Barnaby Jones; episode titled "Focus on Fear" (January 31, 1980). ''[[The Rockford Files]]'', ''[[Good Times]]'', ''[[The Incredible Hulk (1978 TV series)|The Incredible Hulk]]'' and ''[[The Streets of San Francisco]]''. Over the years, Franklin's looks have typically landed him roles portraying men of power, such as members of the police force or military officials. Between 1975 and 1985 Franklin was a regular cast member in four TV series. The first, [[American Broadcasting Company|ABC]]'s ''[[Caribe (U.S. TV series)|Caribe]]'' in 1975, was a law enforcement drama that aired 13 episodes and cast him as police sergeant Mark Walters. Two years later, [[NBC]]'s fantasy-science fiction series ''[[The Fantastic Journey]]'' lasted for 10 episodes, with Franklin as athletic young physician Dr. Fred Walters. After four more years, a two-hour [[television film]], ''[[McClain's Law (film)|McClain's Law]]'', led to Franklin's second police series titled, per the telefilm, ''[[McClain's Law]]'', a modern-day NBC vehicle for ''[[Gunsmoke]]'' star [[James Arness]], with Franklin fifth-billed as police detective Jerry Cross, but the 1981–82 series only lasted 14 episodes. Franklin's longest lasting and most recognizable acting role was his 1983–85 portrayal of Captain Crane on the popular action-adventure series ''[[The A-Team]]''. === Directing === Inspired by the low-budget films of the 1980s, such as ''[[Chan Is Missing]]'' (1982), Franklin enrolled at the [[AFI Conservatory]] in Los Angeles in 1986. His 30-minute [[Master of Fine Arts|M.F.A.]] thesis film ''Punk'' is about an African-American boy in [[South-central Los Angeles]] dealing with his sexuality and manhood.{{Cite web |last=Loynd |first=Ray |date=August 6, 1993 |title=TV REVIEWS : 'Punk': An Odyssey for the Young at Heart |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1993-08-06-ca-20829-story.html |access-date=December 3, 2022 |website=Los Angeles Times |language=en-US}} Straight out of his Master's program, Franklin landed a job with movie producer-director [[Roger Corman]] in 1989. While working at Corman's [[New Concorde|Concorde Films]], Franklin gained experience working on low-budget films, helping to crank out six films in just two years' time. From 1989 to 1990, Franklin worked on ''[[Nowhere to Run (1989 film)|Nowhere to Run]]'', ''[[Eye of the Eagle 2: Inside the Enemy]]'', and ''[[Full Fathom Five (film)|Full Fathom Five]]'', respectively, under Concord Films. At the end of the 80s, producer Jesse Beaton was looking for a director for a film called ''[[One False Move]]''. Remembering Franklin's short film ''Punk'', Beaton met Carl to discuss the film's vision.[https://movies.yahoo.com/movie/contributor/1800019229/bio Carl Franklin Biography - Yahoo! Movies] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110628201618/http://movies.yahoo.com/movie/contributor/1800019229/bio|date=June 28, 2011}} Franklin's approach to the screenplay produced a thriller of the [[film noir]] genre. The story follows three drug dealers, played by [[Billy Bob Thornton]], [[Cynda Williams]], and [[Michael Beach]] and their interactions with a small-town Arkansas police chief played by [[Bill Paxton]]. Far from his low-budget past, Franklin's budget of $2 million gave him a bit of room to be creative, and achieve his entire vision for the film. However, the original version of the film, which was released in 1991, was thought to be overly violent. In response to such claims, Franklin told the ''Observer'', "I didn't want people getting excited seeing how neat someone can be killed... I want the audience to feel the emotional loss of life--the real violence is the loss, the violation of humanity. They've taken from us someone who had dreams, hopes, the same set of emotions we have." Despite the film's lack of professional publicity, ''One False Move'' was largely promoted by word of mouth and earned itself mixed reviews. However, the reviews that were positive were very positive, gaining the project more attention. The film was named Best Film of the Year by [[Gene Siskel]], and one of the 10 Best Films of 1992 by the National Review Board.{{cite journal|jstor=27761553|pages=8|title=BFC/A Hosts Carl Franklin|volume=15|issue=1|journal=Black Camera|year=2000}} Franklin collaborated with producers [[Jonathan Demme]] and Jesse Beaton on adapting [[Walter Mosley]]'s novel ''[[Devil in a Blue Dress]]'' after Demme acquired its film rights. Franklin directed and wrote the screenplay for [[Devil in a Blue Dress (film)|the film]] on a {{Usd|21,000,000}} budget. The film starred [[Denzel Washington]] as [[Ezekiel "Easy" Rawlins]]. Switching to television, Franklin directed ''[[Laurel Avenue]]'', a two-part miniseries focused on an African-American family in [[Minnesota]] for [[HBO]] in 1993. One issue in particular that stood out in the series was the issue of drug use. Franklin defended his depictions, explaining that "Drugs are a huge problem in the black community. Not to include that would be a stupid oversight. But if the subject of drugs is introduced in the context of a hardworking family that has managed to maintain unity, and the audience sees drugs as a threat to that unity, they get a much greater understanding of the problem." Following ''[[Laurel Avenue]]'', Franklin found himself maintaining A-list status, which allowed him to work on bigger and more visible projects, such as 1998's ''[[One True Thing]]''. The film is an adaptation of an autobiographical story by New York journalist [[Anna Quindlen]], following a woman ([[Renée Zellweger]]) with no option but to leave Manhattan for the small town where she was raised when her mother ([[Meryl Streep]]) is diagnosed with cancer. Franklin went on to direct ''[[High Crimes]]'', starring [[Morgan Freeman]] and [[Ashley Judd]], and ''[[Out of Time (2003 film)|Out of Time]]'', which reunited him with ''Devil in a Blue Dress'' star Denzel Washington. Since then, Franklin has largely transitioned to high-profile television work. He has worked on two series produced by [[Steven Spielberg]], directing the [[television pilot|pilot]] of science fiction drama ''[[Falling Skies]]'' and an episode of the [[World War II]] drama ''[[The Pacific (miniseries)|The Pacific]]''. He has also collaborated on two series with [[David Fincher]], directing four episodes each of ''[[House of Cards (American TV series)|House of Cards]]'' and ''[[Mindhunter (TV series)|Mindhunter]]''. Franklin directed multiple critically acclaimed episodes of the HBO series ''[[The Leftovers (TV series)|The Leftovers]]'', across all three of its seasons. His prolific television credits also include ''[[Rome (TV series)|Rome]]'', ''[[The Newsroom (American TV series)|The Newsroom]]'', ''[[Homeland (TV series)|Homeland]]'', ''[[Ray Donovan]]'', and ''[[Dahmer – Monster: The Jeffrey Dahmer Story]]''. In 2023, Franklin expressed interest in someday directing a feature-length film of his [[American Film Institute|AFI]] short ''Punk''.{{cite video |url=https://youtube.com/watch?v=PnYhi85VmVE&si=v2ca_MPDDvs4HtSY |title=Carl Franklin's Closet Picks |date=May 24, 2023 |publisher=[[The Criterion Collection]] |via=[[YouTube]]}} == Unrealized projects == After ''[[Devil in a Blue Dress (film)|Devil in a Blue Dress]]'', Franklin and [[Denzel Washington]] planned to collaborate on a trilogy of films based on the [[Ezekiel "Easy" Rawlins|Easy Rawlins]] character, but this never materialized.{{Cite web |last=Kois |first=Dan |date=July 22, 2022 |title=The 1990s Denzel Mystery That Should've Launched a Franchise |url=https://slate.com/culture/2022/07/carl-franklin-interview-devil-in-a-blue-dress-and-denzel-washington.html |access-date=November 27, 2022 |website=Slate Magazine |language=en}} Around 1996–97, Franklin was attached to direct a film of the [[Russell Banks]] novel ''[[Rule of the Bone]]'', but the project stalled at [[Columbia Pictures|Columbia]]/[[TriStar Pictures|TriStar]].{{cite news|last=Pristin|first=Terry|url=https://www.nytimes.com/1997/11/30/movies/film-an-author-adapts-to-being-adapted.html|title=FILM; An Author Adapts To Being Adapted|newspaper=[[The New York Times]]|date=November 30, 1997|access-date=March 29, 2025}}{{cite web|author1=Mariotti, Greg|first=Wallis, CJ|url=https://cigsandredvines.blogspot.com/2000/04/april-3-2000.html|title=The Definitive Paul Thomas Anderson Resource: April 2000|website=Cigarettes & Coffee|date=April 3, 2000|access-date=March 29, 2025}} Filmmaker [[Paul Thomas Anderson]] allegedly was hired to write the script,{{cite web|last=Konow|first=David|url=https://www.creativescreenwriting.com/boogie-nights/|title="Movies Do Cause Violence!" Paul Thomas Anderson|website=Creative Screenwriting|date=July 8, 2016|orig-date=1998|access-date=March 29, 2025|volume=5|number=1}} later saying "I didn't do a very good job. I didn't really know what I was doing in general, let alone how to adapt a book."{{Citation needed|date=March 2025}} In January 1997, ''Variety'' indicated that Franklin was set to direct a [[Thriller film|thriller]] for [[Fox 2000]] about ex-[[spy]] [[Aldrich Ames]].{{cite magazine|author=Variety Staff|url=https://variety.com/1997/scene/vpage/day-spikes-fox-s-year-fox-parts-total-some-whole-1117433896/|title='Day' spikes Fox's year Fox parts total some whole|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=January 6, 1997|access-date=January 26, 2025}} The film was titled ''Killer Spy'', with [[Nicolas Cage]] reportedly being courted by the studio for the main role,{{cite magazine|last=Fleming|first=Michael|url=https://variety.com/1997/voices/columns/blue-boy-caruso-cops-deal-for-double-duty-1117433556/|title='Blue' boy Caruso cops deal for double duty|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=January 13, 1997|access-date=January 26, 2025}} though [[Al Pacino]] was later attached. By June, Franklin had left the project, with [[James Gray (director)|James Gray]] entering negotiations to direct in his place.{{cite magazine|last=Busch|first=Anita M.|url=https://variety.com/1997/film/news/gray-in-talks-to-helm-fox-s-ames-pic-1116680078/|title=Gray in talks to helm Fox's Ames pic|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=June 2, 1997|access-date=September 14, 2023}} In June 1997, it was reported that Franklin had dropped out of directing ''[[Brokedown Palace]]'', citing "creative differences" over the casting of the film.{{cite magazine|last=Petrikin|first=Chris|url=https://variety.com/1997/film/news/franklin-out-as-director-of-palace-1116678813/|title=Franklin out as director of 'Palace'|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=June 25, 1997|access-date=January 11, 2024}} [[Jonathan Kaplan]] took over for Franklin following his departure.{{cite magazine|author=Variety Staff|url=https://variety.com/1997/film/news/kaplan-to-take-lease-on-palace-1116675404/|title=Kaplan to take lease on 'Palace'|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=September 3, 1997|access-date=January 11, 2024}} In 1999, Franklin was attached as the director of the sci-fi film ''[[The Mothman Prophecies (film)|The Mothman Prophecies]]'', with [[Richard Gere]] starring, before [[Mark Pellington]] was chosen.{{cite magazine|last=Petrikin|first=Chris|url=https://variety.com/1999/film/news/fox-puts-armitage-in-doud-s-body-1117500041/|title=Fox puts Armitage in Doud's 'Body'|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=May 5, 1999|access-date=January 11, 2024}} Franklin was attached to direct [[Will Smith]] in the fourth remake of the musical ''[[A Star Is Born (1937 film)|A Star Is Born]]'' for [[Warner Bros.]], though Smith passed up the role in order to star in ''[[Ali (2001 film)|Ali]]''.{{cite magazine|last=Angulo|first=Sandra P.|url=https://ew.com/article/2000/09/15/jamie-foxx-planning-remake-star-born/|title=Jamie Foxx is planning to remake ''A Star Is Born''|magazine=[[Entertainment Weekly]]|date=September 15, 2000|access-date=January 11, 2024}} In 2000, Franklin was expected to begin filming ''The Shooter'', an adaptation of ''[[Point of Impact (Stephen Hunter novel)|Point of Impact]]'' by [[Stephen Hunter]]. However, he stepped down as the director and writer of the project, which at the time was planned as a co-production between [[Paramount Pictures]] and [[Lakeshore Entertainment]].{{cite magazine|author=Variety Staff|url=https://variety.com/2000/film/news/inside-moves-142-1117775624/|title=Inside moves|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=January 26, 2000|access-date=January 26, 2025}} In 2001, Franklin was announced to direct and produce a film adaptation of the novel ''Rescue Me'', by [[Gigi Levangie]], who sold the rights to [[Fox Searchlight]]. As of the announcement, no screenwriter was attached to adapt the story.{{cite magazine|last=Bing|first=Jonathan|url=https://variety.com/2001/film/news/fox-mounts-grazer-rescue-1117793780/|title=Fox mounts Grazer 'Rescue'|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=February 14, 2001|access-date=January 11, 2024}} In 2002, it was reported that writer Sid Quashie was tapped by [[Paramount Pictures]] to adapt Susan Kelly's 1995 book ''The Boston Stranglers'', with Franklin attached to direct. The film was scheduled to go into production that summer, with [[Gale Anne Hurd]] and Jesse Beaton producing.{{cite magazine|author1=Dunkley, Cathy|author2=Harris, Dana|url=https://variety.com/2002/film/news/boston-baking-at-par-1117859173/|title='Boston' baking at Par|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=January 27, 2002|access-date=January 11, 2024}} In 2003, Franklin was set to direct the legal thriller ''[[The Emperor of Ocean Park]]'' for Warner Bros. Pictures from the novel by [[Stephen L. Carter]], adapted by [[Stephen Schiff]].{{cite magazine|author1=Dunkley, Cathy|url=https://variety.com/2003/film/markets-festivals/helmer-gives-park-sparks-1117889374/|title=Helmer gives 'Park' sparks|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=July 15, 2003|access-date=January 11, 2024}} In early 2007, Franklin had been attached to direct the legal drama ''Tulia'' for [[Lionsgate Films]], starring [[Halle Berry]] and [[Billy Bob Thornton]]. Karen Croner wrote the script for the film, based on the [[Nate Blakeslee]] book ''Tulia: Race, Cocaine, and Corruption in a Small Texas Town''. In August that year, [[John Singleton]] took over directing duties from Franklin, who departed from the project.{{cite magazine|last=McNary|first=Dave|url=https://variety.com/2007/film/markets-festivals/john-singleton-to-direct-tulia-1117969579/|title=John Singleton to direct 'Tulia'|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=August 1, 2007|access-date=January 11, 2024}} The film was not made. On July 23, 2007, it was reported that Franklin would direct ''The Maintenance Man'', the [[Screen Gems]] adaptation of [[Michael Baisden]]'s novel about a [[gigolo]] in existential crisis, set to begin shooting later that year.{{cite magazine|last=Fleming|first=Michael|url=https://variety.com/2007/film/markets-festivals/carl-franklin-to-direct-maintenance-1117969031/|title=Carl Franklin to direct 'Maintenance'|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=July 23, 2007|access-date=January 11, 2024}} On July 31, 2007, it was reported that Franklin would direct ''Snitch'' for [[New Line Cinema]], a thriller produced by Guy East and [[Nigel Sinclair]] inspired by true events chronicled in a [[PBS]] ''[[Frontline (American TV program)|Frontline]]'' documentary. [[Justin Haythe]], who wrote the screenplay, was to executive produce the film along with Franklin's producing partner Jesse Beaton.{{cite web|last=Kit|first=Borys|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/business/business-news/true-story-franklin-set-snitch-145539/|title=True story: Franklin set to 'Snitch'|website=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|date=July 31, 2007|access-date=January 11, 2024}} In 2009, [[HBO]] was developing a historical [[miniseries]] from Franklin about the [[Black Panther Party]] called ''The Black Panthers'', which he was writing and attached to direct and executive produce.{{cite magazine|last=Schneider|first=Michael|url=https://variety.com/2009/scene/markets-festivals/hbo-channels-historical-miniseries-1118008605/|title=HBO channels historical miniseries|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=September 14, 2009|access-date=January 26, 2025}} He later further developed it as a project for [[Netflix]].{{cite web|url=https://www.fxnetworks.com/shows/american-sports-story/aaron-hernandez/crew/carl-franklin-executive-producer|title=Carl Franklin | Executive Producer | American Sports Story on FX|website=[[FX (TV channel)|FX]]|access-date=January 26, 2025}} On February 8, 2011, [[Peter Facinelli]] was reported to write the script for, star in and co-produce the [[Independent film|indie]] crime drama ''El Chico Blanco'', with Franklin directing. Titan Worldwide Entertainment was financing the project, which would have been shot in [[New Mexico]].{{cite magazine|last=Sneider|first=Jeff|url=https://variety.com/2011/film/news/facinelli-to-star-in-indie-drama-he-wrote-1118031781/|title=Facinelli to star in indie drama he wrote|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=February 8, 2011|access-date=January 11, 2024}} On May 29, 2012, Meyers Media Group and McDonald Entertainment announced that they would co-finance the thriller ''City of Night'', to be directed by Franklin, written by David Chisholm and produced by Brendan McDonald. Set against the backdrop of [[South Los Angeles|South Central L.A.]], the film follows a rookie cop who becomes the target of an elaborate psychological game to destroy him. A date for principal photography was soon to be announced,{{cite web|author=The Deadline Team|url=https://deadline.com/2012/05/carl-franklin-to-helm-city-of-night-278978/|title=Carl Franklin To Helm 'City of Night'|website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]|date=May 29, 2012|access-date=January 11, 2024}} but the project did not move forward. In March 2013, it was reported that Franklin would direct a [[Biographical film|biopic]] about the life of [[soul music]] singer/songwriter [[Sam Cooke]]. [[ABKCO Records]] was set to independently produce the project.{{cite web|last=Jagernauth|first=Kevin|url=https://theplaylist.net/carl-franklin-to-direct-biopic-about-soul-music-legend-sam-cooke-20130327/|title=Carl Franklin To Direct Biopic About Soul Music Legend Sam Cooke|website=The Playlist|date=March 27, 2013|access-date=January 11, 2024}} As of 2015, Franklin was still developing the film, which was then in the process of being cast from a script he wrote himself, based on [[Peter Guralnick]]'s biography ''Dream Boogie: The Triumph of Sam Cooke''.{{cite web|last=Kit|first=Borys|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/news/general-news/sam-cooke-getting-biopic-treatment-782557/|title=Sam Cooke Getting Biopic Treatment (Exclusive)|website=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|date=March 17, 2015|access-date=January 11, 2024}} In April 2015, Franklin replaced John Singleton as director of Morgan Creek's ''Tupac'', a biopic written by Jeremy Haft and Ed Gonzalez about rapper [[Tupac Shakur]]. Casting for the role was reportedly under way, with principal photography planned to begin in August or September.{{cite magazine|last=McNary|first=Dave|url=https://variety.com/2015/film/news/tupac-movie-director-carl-franklin-john-singleton-1201468767/|title=Carl Franklin to Direct 'Tupac' Movie, Replacing John Singleton|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=April 8, 2015|access-date=January 11, 2024}} In May 2016, Franklin was announced to be directing a film adaptation of [[William Faulkner]]'s ''[[Intruder in the Dust]]''. Our House Productions held the rights to produce the adaptation of the 1948 novel, with distribution rights for the project being sold at [[2019 Cannes Film Festival|that year's Cannes Film Festival]].{{cite magazine|last=McNary|first=Dave|url=https://variety.com/2016/film/festivals/carl-franklin-intruder-in-the-dust-adaptation-1201778110/|title=Cannes: Carl Franklin Directing 'Intruder in the Dust' Adaptation (EXCLUSIVE)|magazine=[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]|date=May 18, 2016|access-date=January 11, 2024}} In July 2016, [[John Malkovich]] signed on to star in and executive produce ''Humboldt'', a TV drama series to be directed by Franklin, inspired by Emily Brady's best-selling book ''[[Humboldt: Life on America's Marijuana Frontier]]''. The project was written on [[Spec script|spec]] by [[Michael Alan Lerner|Michael A. Lerner]], and set up at [[Sony Pictures Television]] and [[Anonymous Content]].{{cite web|last=Goldberg|first=Lesley|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-news/john-malkovich-star-marijuana-drama-915115/|title=John Malkovich to Star in Marijuana Drama Series|website=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|date=July 27, 2016|access-date=January 11, 2024}} Despite Franklin's prolific career in television, this never came to fruition either. In 2018, it was reported that Franklin was prepping to direct ''Excessive Force'', a thriller about racism and corruption in the [[Cleveland]] [[police department]] written by [[Jeff Kwatinetz]] and [[Ice Cube]] and set to star Cube in the main role. The film was planned to enter production that fall, produced under Cube's production banner CubeVision.{{cite web|last=Busch|first=Anita|url=https://deadline.com/2018/04/excessive-force-ice-cube-carl-franklin-cubevision-slate-1202375733/|title='Excessive Force,' Carl Franklin To Direct With Ice Cube Starring, Is Latest On CubeVision Slate|website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]|date=April 24, 2018|access-date=January 24, 2025}} In 2022, Franklin was attached to the series ''Black Harvest'', set in Paris in 1952, as [[executive producer]]. The project was developed with Epix Studios.{{cite web|last=White|first=Peter|url=https://deadline.com/2022/02/kevin-kline-theater-comedy-cocaine-chris-brancato-epix-1234925548/|title=Kevin Kline Theater Comedy & Cocaine Drama From Chris Brancato In Works At Epix|website=[[Deadline Hollywood]]|date=February 3, 2022|access-date=March 30, 2025}} ==Race and film== Franklin says "I am interested in the universal values of the black experience." Discussing the realities for black Americans in the television and film industry, Franklin said: "When I came up, the only legitimate dramatic actor was [[Sidney Poitier]], the bankable star was [[Richard Pryor]] and the other choice roles were action parts that went to [[Jim Brown]]. Carl Michael Franklin (born April 11, 1949) is an American film and television director, producer, screenwriter, and former actor. He began his career in the 1970s as a television actor, playing regular roles as Dr. Fred Walters on The Fantastic Journey, Detective Jerry Cross on McClain's Law, and Captain Crane on The A-Team. In the 1980s, he graduated from the AFI Conservatory, and began directing B-movies at Roger Corman's Concorde Pictures.
His 1992 film One False Move (1992), written by and starring Billy Bob Thornton, earned him the Best Director Award at the 8th Independent Spirit Awards. His subsequent cinematic directorial efforts include Devil in a Blue Dress and Out of Time; both starring Denzel Washington, One True Thing, High Crimes, and Bless Me, Ultima. 
Since the 2010s, most of his work has been for television, including shows such as: Rome, The Pacific, The Newsroom, House of Cards, Homeland, The Affair, The Leftovers, 13 Reasons Why, Ray Donovan, Mindhunter, and the Ryan Murphy production Monster. His television accolades include a BAFTA TV Award, two NAACP Image Awards, and two Primetime Emmy Award nominations.
